parts.solution_md:
Liquidity has weakened as the current ratio fell from 2.1:1 in 2025 to 1.29:1 in 2026. In 2026, current assets totalled £310k compared to £240k of current liabilities, whereas in 2025 the gap was much larger (£340k vs £160k) **[Ap]**. This means SSH has less working capital available to cover short-term debts. Managers will face tougher decisions about paying suppliers or investing in new staff, as cash reserves are now lower. This increases the risk of liquidity problems, reducing flexibility in day-to-day decision-making** [An]**

Receivables have increased while cash has fallen. Trade receivables are £30k higher, while cash is £30k lower compared with 2025 **[Ap]**. More money is tied up in customers not yet paying, creating slower cash inflows **[K]**. This weakens liquidity further, meaning SSH may need to chase payments urgently or use the overdraft to fund operations. Managers may delay hiring or training decisions until cash becomes available, reducing the firm’s ability to expand quickly** [An]**

The business is also now reliant on an overdraft **[Ap]**. SSH took out a new £50k overdraft in 2026, alongside £30k higher payables **[Ap]**. The overdraft provides short-term relief for paying suppliers, but it adds interest costs. This makes decision-making riskier, as managers must balance the need for immediate liquidity with the long-term impact of higher expenses. If interest rates rise again, the cost of this decision could increase** [An]**

The most significant issue is the rise in receivables, as this directly slows down the inflow of cash needed for daily operations **[E]**. While the overdraft helps in the short term, it is only a temporary fix. Weakening liquidity ratios are concerning, but they are partly a result of the receivables problem. Therefore, tightening credit control and chasing payments should be the priority over alternatives such as delaying recruitment or packaging investment, as recovering cash will improve liquidity and decision-making flexibility **[E]**

parts.problem_md: **Explain **why liquidity and profitability are important to a business.
parts.solution_md:
Liquidity is a signal that a business will be able to pay back its short-term debts **[K]**, such as money owed to suppliers, workers' wages or fixed costs, such as rent **[An]**. If a business does not pay these debts, it would likely fail very quickly **[An]**. Without inventory or raw materials, staff to produce output, or a location in which to produce, it would have nothing to sell and would cease trading **[An]**

Profitability measures how well profit is being made from sales or capital invested in the business **[K]**. A profitable business will have  funds to reinvest in the business, perhaps to be used to fund expansion **[An]**. It is, therefore, a measure of success and also of business potential, in which banks and investors are often very interested **[An]** as it demonstrates that a business can provide a return either on the capital investors put in, or shares bought **[An]**

> - In each paragraph:

>   - Apply it clearly to the case study → 1 Ap mark
>   - Explain how it works using a cause–effect chain → up to 2 An marks
>

> 
> - Liquidity:
> 
>   - Allows a business to see if it is able to pay back the short-term debts of the business
>   - Measured by current ratio/acid test ratio
>   - If it cannot pay the debts, then it will not be able to buy more inventory or raw materials
>   - If the business becomes illiquid it may be forced to sell business assets to pay debts and will cease trading
> - Profitability:
> 
>   - It measures how well profit is being made from sales or capital invested in the business
>   - Could be used to reinvest into the business/use retained profits for expansion
>   - Measured by gross profit margin/profit margin/ROCE
>   - It can be a measure of efficiency
>   - Can compare business performance over time/compare against other businesses
>   - It helps investors or bank to decide whether to invest in the business or lend it money
>   - Retain shareholders/pay dividends/return on investment for the owners

**Summary of CC’s financial information from the end of the second year of trading (\$)**

| Revenue | 800 000 |
|---|---|

| Gross profit | 400 000 |
| Expenses | 250 000 |

Using the data in Appendix 3, **calculate **the following ratios for CC:

- Profit margin

Show your workings.

parts.solution_md:
**Gross profit margin = 50%** **[2]**

**Profit margin = 18.75% ****[2]**

**Current ratio = 1.33** **[2]**

**Acid test ratio = 1 ****[2]**

**Calculation steps**

Calculate the gross profit margin by dividing gross profit by revenue, then multiplying the outcome by 100

$\mathrm{Gross} \mathrm{profit} \mathrm{margin}-\frac{\mathrm{Gross} \mathrm{profit}}{\mathrm{Revenue}}\times100$    **[1]**

$= \frac{\$ 400 , 000}{\$ 800 , 000} \times 100

= 50 \%$    **[1]**

Calculate the profit margin by dividing profit by revenue, then multiplying the outcome by 100

$\mathrm{Profit} \mathrm{margin}-\frac{\mathrm{Profit}}{\mathrm{Revenue}}\times100$    **[1]**

$= \frac{\$ 150 , 000}{\$ 800 , 000} \times 100

= 18.75 \%$    **[1]**

Calculate the current ratio by dividing current assets by current liabilities

$\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{ratio}=\frac{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{assets}}{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{liabilities}}$    **[1]**

$= \$ 20 , 000 \div \$ 15 , 000

= 1.33$    **[1]**

Calculate the acid test ratio by subtracting inventory from current assets, then dividing the outcome by current liabilities

$\text{Acid} \text{test} \text{ratio} = \frac{ ( \text{Current} \text{assets} - \text{Inventory} )}{Current liabilities}$    **[1]**

$= ( \$ 20 , 000 - \$ 5 , 000 ) \div \$ 15 , 000

= 1.00$     **[1]**
